blocks.text: HTTP is a message contract: the method expresses intent, the path identifies a resource, headers describe the exchange, status classifies the result, and the body carries the representation. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. This separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: An envelope carries address and instructions, a receipt reports success or trouble, and the enclosed letter is the body.

GET reads, POST creates or triggers, PUT/PATCH replace or modify, and DELETE removes; the server must still enforce actual semantics and authorization. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

2xx statuses indicate success, 4xx a request or authorization problem, and 5xx a server failure. response.ok covers 200–299, but fetch does not automatically reject a 404 response. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

Content-Type describes the sent format and Accept the desired format. response.json() should be called only when the body actually contains valid JSON. blocks.text: DNS translates a stable name into routing information, TCP reaches a service on a port, and TLS authenticates the server and encrypts the channel before HTTP flows. Each layer solves a distinct problem. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. This separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: DNS is the directory, the IP address the building, the port the office number, and TLS the identity check plus sealed conversation.

An A record points to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, and CNAME aliases another name. Changes are cached for their TTL and therefore do not become universal instantly. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

localhost bypasses public DNS and targets your machine; port 3000 selects the development server. In production, HTTPS normally uses 443 and the platform then routes to the application. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

The TLS certificate must cover the requested name and chain to a trusted authority. HTTPS protects transport but does not automatically make server code authorized or flawless. Finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. Short changes make cause and effect easy to connect.
